title: Oil Prices Caught Between a Looming Glut and Middle East Turmoil
summary: Oil prices have traded in a narrow range over the past few sessions as forecasts of a coming surplus collide with continued attacks and stalled diplomacy in the Middle East. body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Oil prices have traded in a narrow range over the past few sessions as forecasts of a coming surplus collide with continued attacks and stalled diplomacy in the Middle East. A run of agency reports this month has pushed expectations toward oversupply and weighed on crude. Brent crude was up 0.22% at $92.18 per barrel in early trade on Friday, well below its October levels above $110 but little changed from the start of the week, while WTI crude had gained 0.35% to $82.73 per barrel. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November Oil Market Report that the global oil market will return to surplus in the fourth quarter as Gulf exports recover faster than global demand. Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels per day in October, and the agency now sees supply exceeding demand by 1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026, a swing from its previous forecast of a 1.8 million bpd deficit. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3 million bpd from last month, cut its 2027 demand forecast by 80,000 bpd to 104.3 million bpd, and lowered the implied call on OPEC crude by 220,000 bpd to 20.8 million bpd. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has moved in the same direction . In October, it forecast a 700,000 bpd inventory draw in the fourth quarter. It now expects stocks to build in Q4 and to rise by an average of 3.5 million bpd in the first half of 2027, after drawing down for most of this year. The EIA estimates that crude production shut in across the Gulf fell to 2.5 million bpd in October, from 4.8 million bpd in September and a peak of 10.9 million bpd in May. OPEC said crude output from the OPEC+ alliance rose by roughly 2 million bpd in October, led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Analysts at Standard Chartered caution that higher Gulf output does not yet mean more oil reaching buyers. Tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure and record freight rates are still holding back shipments, and inventories drained earlier this year have left little cushion. The bank also warns that the IEA’s surplus call is larger than any other agency’s, and that forecast surpluses in the past have often failed to arrive on schedule. The agencies also disagree on demand. OPEC’s November report puts global oil demand at 108.3 million bpd in 2027, almost 4 million bpd above the IEA’s figure, and keeps its forecast for 2027 demand growth at 2.55 million bpd. The two agencies measure liquids differently, so the gap overstates the disagreement, but it remains wide. The IEA expects petrochemical feedstocks to drive most of next year’s growth, with little increase in gasoline and diesel use. The EIA expects global liquids demand to grow by 2 million bpd in 2027 after falling by about the same amount this year. Standard Chartered says the demand question will decide how much of the returning Gulf supply the market can absorb. OPEC’s higher consumption forecast leaves room for far more barrels than the IEA’s. The bank expects continued attacks on shipping, maritime security risks and stalled talks to keep a geopolitical premium in prices and sustain volatility, but still sees crude prices falling through 2027 as the market slowly normalizes. In natural gas, Standard Chartered expects European prices to hold at elevated levels through winter, even if milder weather on the continent and better LNG supply bring short-term relief. Europe has already drawn heavily on storage that started the season low: EU gas inventories stood at 70.4% on Nov. 15, about 18 percentage points below the five-year average. Qatar’s LNG exports roughly doubled in October from September but remain about two-thirds below their pre-war level, and QatarEnergy’s force majeure on European deliveries runs through December. Colder weather in Britain could also pull gas away from the continent, so Europe will still need steady imports to protect what is left in storage. Dutch TTF front-month

body: Rystad Energy is an independent energy consulting services and business intelligence provider offering global databases, strategic advisory and research products for energy companies and suppliers,… Starting in January, Democratic governors will lead US states that together hold 77% of the 300 gigawatts (GW) of data center capacity announced for 2027-2030, including the five largest markets: Texas, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Georgia. Most of the winning candidates campaigned on making data centers pay their grid costs, rather than on stopping them, so the midterms are likely to change the terms of growth more than its pace. Our risked forecast expects 121 GW to be added in 2027-2030, including about 49 GW of the 191 GW planned for 2029-30. Texas had implemented a permit pause but lifted it on 17 November at the behest of outgoing Governor Greg Abbott. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to implement a new one which, if it lasts until new rules take effect in September 2027, will delay about 3 GW of capacity. If the pauses are sustained for another year, over 10 GW is pushed back, and installed capacity at the end of 2029 would be about 170 GW instead of 177 GW. We expect most of the delayed capacity to be online by the end of 2030. Pauses delay little, and mostly in Texas. Most moratoria across the US stop or delay only projects that are still awaiting approval. About half of the capacity planned for 2027-28 is already under construction or roofed. Of the planned capacity we expect, 16% still needs approval and is thus exposed to political changes. Slow construction already pushes nearly a third of the capacity we expect for 2027-28 past its planned year, far more than the pauses delay. Texas's permit pause has ended, but a new one may follow. Texas's environmental regulator, TCEQ, stopped issuing data center permits in September but resumed its reviews on 17 November, two weeks after Abbott lost his bid for a fourth term. The grid operator, ERCOT, has paused approvals for new large data center connections since August, pending ERCOT’s audit report, due by 10 December, and the state utility regulator's meeting on 17 December. Hinojosa has pledged a new moratorium from 19 January until the Texas State Legislature passes protections in its upcoming session, which ends on 31 May. The window requires developers to act early. Most of the Texas data center projects we expect would be caught up in a new permitting pause. However, some developers now have reason to file for stormwater cover ahead of need, which would let them clear land before a potential new pause. That would mean between 1.5 and 3 GW of capacity would be delayed; if Texas opts not to implement a new permitting pause, about 1 GW will be delayed nationwide. The lasting change is the cost of reserving grid capacity, and it has bipartisan support. Utilities increasingly require commitments of more than a decade and upfront security. Virginia, for example, will require 14-year commitments and collateral of up to $1.5 million per megavolt-ampere for contracts signed from January. Such rules cover states with over half of planned capacity, and pending or promised rules would extend them to about three-quarters. They weigh most on speculative projects, which must commit for years before they know the capacity will be used. Rystad Energy’s data center risk assessment has largely risked them out of our prior forecast, and the midterm results strengthen the odds that they will not progress. Onsite power is no escape in Texas. About half of Texas's planned capacity will be in data centers that will generate their own power, either fully behind-the-meter or as a hybrid with a grid connection. TCEQ's pause applied to these projects, for air permits as well as the stormwater permits all projects need, and ERCOT's hold still applies to campuses that also draw on the grid. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… Japan plans to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude for the national petroleum reserve it drew down during the Hormuz crisis, under a deal the two countries announced on Friday that makes the purchases subject to favorable market conditions. The deal also gives Saudi Arabia temporary use of an additional 16 million barrels of storage capacity in Japan, expanding the 8 million barrels it already holds there, and the kingdom has begun refilling those tanks, Bloomberg reported. Under the existing arrangement with Saudi Aramco, Japan gets preferential rights to purchase the Saudi crude stored in its facilities during a supply emergency. Aramco can sell that oil to other Asian customers under normal conditions, but Japan gets first access when supplies are disrupted. Middle Eastern crude made up more than 90% of Japan’s imports before the war. When Iranian attacks all but shut the Strait of Hormuz, Japan bought cargoes from as far away as Canada, Azerbaijan and Africa to keep its refiners running. Tokyo released oil from its national reserves last month as part of the International Energy Agency’s coordinated drawdown, in which member countries agreed to release a record 400 million barrels. Gulf crude exports recovered to 82% of prewar levels in October, according to the IEA , and the question for the market now is when importers will start buying back what they released. Brent traded around $92 a barrel on Thursday, down from above $110 in October, and Goldman Sachs expects a sizable surplus next year that will push prices lower. Producers are building their own buffers closer to their customers. Saudi Arabia has held talks with foreign governments to give Aramco access to their strategic storage, and Singapore announced plans last month to store Saudi crude in its Jurong Rock Caverns during the second half of 2027. Tokyo wants a regional system on top of the bilateral deals. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi this week proposed a joint Asian task force to manage crude stockpiles, which she described as an Asian version of the IEA . ASEAN members have separately agreed on a shared reserve with storage sites in Indonesia and Thailand, coordinated by the Philippines. body: Europe’s biggest airline group, Lufthansa, plans to eliminate as many as 1,000 jobs and reduce capacity on short and medium-haul destinations, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing a letter to employees it had seen. Lufthansa and all other airlines have struggled this year with increasing pressure on profits from soaring fuel prices amid the Middle East conflict. Spiking crude and jet fuel prices are adding billions of dollars to every air carrier’s fuel costs. In early November, Lufthansa Group said that “strong demand and cost discipline more than offset higher fuel costs,” but it still guided for a massive fuel bill for the year. In the third quarter alone, fuel costs jumped by $596 million (543 million euros) compared with the prior-year quarter. Due to the unchanged geopolitical situation, Lufthansa Group’s expected fuel bill for the full year is rising to $10.2 billion (9.3 billion euros), according to Till Streichert, chief financial officer of Deutsche Lufthansa AG. “However, with a hedging ratio for our passenger airlines of around 86 percent for 2026 and already more than 60 percent for 2027, we are well positioned relative to the market,” the executive said early this month. A few weeks later, reports by Bloomberg and German news agencies and outlets circulated on Friday that Lufthansa plans to eliminate full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further slash capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and reduce its Airbus A320 aircraft fleet, turning to the smaller Airbus A220, according to the letter from the management to employees. Lufthansa in April slashed a total of 20,000 short-haul flights from its European summer schedule amid concerns about jet fuel shortages and soaring fuel prices. The airline industry faces further months of difficulties as jet fuel prices remain very high and hedging contracts are expiring . Most airlines, including in the U.S., will report losses this year, and some air carriers elsewhere may not survive the winter. title: Copper price sinks into bear market, erasing 2026 gains in worst week of the year
summary: AI’s pull on copper was “a bit over-egged”, says Benchmark, and the metal piled up in the US on tariff bets is now being shipped to China, where traders are paying $500 premiums.
body: AI’s pull on copper was “a bit over-egged”, says Benchmark, and the metal piled up in the US on tariff bets is now being shipped to China, where traders are paying $500 premiums. Copper slumped again on Friday, tipping the metal into a bear market just ten weeks after it set an all-time high, as the unwinding of bets on the artificial intelligence boom, a strong dollar and fading US tariff prospects continued to swamp evidence of acute shortage in China. Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, dropped as much as 3.4% to $5.4405 a pound ($11,994 a tonne), the lowest since the end of March, before recovering to $5.4995 around midday, down 2.4%. That is 20.2% below the record settlement of $6.8885 reached on September 9. A close under $5.51 would meet the common definition of a bear market, a fall of 20% or more from the most recent peak. The contract has fallen for seven sessions in a row and is down more than 9% since last Friday, by far its steepest weekly loss of 2026. A year-to-date gain that stood at 22% in September has turned into a loss of 2%, and copper is on course to end November about 15% lower. On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper fell 2.3% to $12,235 a tonne in official trading after touching $12,020, the lowest since March 24, Reuters reports. The benchmark is down about 9% on the week, its biggest weekly fall since early April 2025, when US President Donald Trump unveiled his global tariffs. London copper is 18% below its September 10 peak of $14,875 and would have to drop under $11,900 to join New York in a bear market. In Shanghai, futures racked up their worst week in 15 years, according to Bloomberg. The break below $5.63, where copper ended 2025, removes the first of two chart supports that Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen flagged during Wednesday’s rout . The second is $5.32, which sits just beneath the lowest close of 2026: $5.34 on March 20, when surging oil prices during the Iran war and swelling exchange inventories sent the metal to a three-month trough. Copper is now less than 3% above that level. Evidence is mounting that the AI investment boom is waning and that the Federal Reserve will have to get more aggressive to control inflation, Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, told Reuters, adding that a strengthening dollar is also weighing on the metal. AI shares continued to sag on Friday, with Anthropic trading about 9% below Thursday’s close after its market debut, the news agency said. “We have been saying for as long as AI has been driving the price that this might be a bit over-egged,” Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Bloomberg. Weak Chinese demand, the dimming prospect of US tariffs and the dollar are also at work, and the week’s losses are not far off the slumps seen in the early stages of the pandemic and after Trump’s Liberation Day announcement. London copper is heading for its steepest monthly decline since 2022 . The selloff in futures is still running alongside a scramble for physical metal in China. The Yangshan premium paid to import copper into the country slipped to $495 a tonne on Friday from Thursday’s record $500, Reuters reports. It was $360 on Wednesday and less than $100 in September. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks rose by 3,204 tonnes this week to 30,846 tonnes, which is still less than a day’s worth of Chinese consumption. That tightness may be part of what is pushing futures down. Premiums at these levels have made it profitable to move metal out of the United States, where stockpiles ballooned over the past year on tariff bets, and traders have begun shipping copper from the US to China , with tens of thousands of tonnes due to arrive in January. Codelco is meanwhile offering Chinese buyers 2027 cathode at $250 to $280 a tonne , less than it charged this year. The flow looks set to continue. title: Ground View Pakistan: The smelter before the mine
summary: Pakistan's push to refine minerals at home faces a copper processing glut, scarce mine supply and financing challenges.
body: Pakistan's push to refine minerals at home faces a copper processing glut, scarce mine supply and financing challenges. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. ( Image courtesy of President.az, CC BY 4.0. ) Pakistan’s ambition to build a domestic copper processing industry risks putting smelters ahead of mines at a time when global refining capacity already exceeds available concentrate supplies. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reinforced that ambition at the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum (PMIF) in Islamabad, pledging to end exports of unprocessed minerals and calling for Reko Diq and other projects in the southwest to support refineries, smelters and factories producing cables and conductors. “Mine in Pakistan, process in Pakistan, manufacture in Pakistan and then export to the rest of the world,” Sharif said. The push reflects a desire to capture more jobs, skills and export revenue from Pakistan’s mineral wealth. But with only one producing copper operation, at Saindak, and its flagship Reko Diq project still awaiting commercial production, the country faces a more immediate challenge: establishing reliable mine output before committing billions to processing infrastructure. Ahsan Iqbal, Pakistan’s federal minister of planning, development and special initiatives, said the government now asks investors to submit complete value-chain proposals rather than plans focused solely on extraction and raw-material exports. That requirement creates a particular challenge for explorers. Copper smelters are designed around specific concentrates, including their grades, impurities and expected volumes. title: Modern Mining targets 40,000 gold ounces from e-waste
summary: The resource-recovery company is turning its tested method into a US production hub following a $40-million IPO.
body: The resource-recovery company is turning its tested method into a US production hub following a $40-million IPO. Modern Mining Technology (NYSE American: MDRN) has laid out a 18-month plan to use its resource recovery from e-waste technology and its first commercial-scale operation in North Carolina, set to produce 40,000 gold equivalent ounces. The company outlined a three-phase development plan , following the closing of its $40-million initial public offering on Nov. 12. The project will use an aqueous-based process to recover gold, silver, copper and other metals from electronic waste. “We approach electronic waste with the mindset of a mining company, as an above-ground resource rather than simply a waste stream,” Modern Mining CEO Jeet Basi, said. The company has tested the technology and commercial viability of the process in its pilot plant, where it has recovered and sold metal concentrate since November 2023. It set 41 product lots between December 2023 and June 2026 in the demonstration facility in Greenville, North Carolina. The idea now is to use the pilot plant as a model to develop commercial scale metals recovery. Shares in Modern Mining were down 1.49% to $2.31 apiece by mid-day Friday in New York, valuing the company at $77.6 million. During the first six to nine months, Modern Mining aims to complete construction of a pre-concentration plant and an aqueous purification plant. The company said supply contracts with recyclers, e-waste aggregators and manufacturers will be secured and training will also be completed. In the first year, Modern Mining aims to start ramping up toward the pre-concentration plant’s capacity of one tonne of waste printed circuit boards per hour. From then until month 18 of the plan to keep expanding commercial production and revenue. “Building our first commercial-scale plant is the step that turns that resource into a new source of supply for the US market,” Basi said. “We designed our model so that each pre-concentration plant we add can feed the same purification hub, giving us a clear path to growth.” The company also intends to pursue R2 Standard certification for responsible electronics recycling as it develops the operation. Modern Mining estimates its process can produce metal grades about 100 times higher than those found in traditionally mined ores. It says the technology could offer a cleaner, safer and lower-cost alternative to conventional mining, although those advantages have yet to be demonstrated at commercial scale. Future pre-concentration plants will be located near electronic waste suppliers to reduce transportation expenses and improve efficiency. Modern Mining plans to expand and research how to improve recovery rates and evaluate additional metals and feedstocks to be integrated in the process.

International copper futures prices have plunged recently, while prices on the Shanghai market have surged as Chinese inventories dwindled. Moves by the US government toward imposing tariffs on copper are pulling large volumes of physical metal into the United States and distorting global distribution flows. Reuters reported on November 20 that three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange fell 6% on November 18 to $12,379.50 a ton, the lowest level in seven months. Weaker expectations for artificial-intelligence investment, a stronger dollar and economic uncertainty added to the downward pressure. Copper is used in electrical wiring for data centers. The November copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange jumped more than 9% on November 16, the contract’s expiration date, to 118,060 yuan a ton. The surge was driven by a shortage of physical copper available to cover short futures positions. Deliverable inventories on the exchange plunged to 27,642 tons this month from 433,458 tons in March. Only 2,270 tons were available for settlement of the November contract. The inventory shortage squeezed traders holding short positions and triggered an unusual spike ahead of expiration. Market moves tied to US tariff policy created the imbalance. Last year, the US Commerce Department said it would impose a 15% tariff on copper imports early next year and raise the rate to 30% in 2028. The tariff threat has fueled demand to bring copper into the United States for storage in advance, since prices there could rise above overseas markets once the levy takes effect. Delivery premiums in the US market have also climbed. As a result, global copper shipments are being funneled into the US market. Data from the World Bureau of Metal Statistics show US copper imports surged 80% from a year earlier to 1.64 million tons last year. body: WASHINGTON – Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson believes the US central bank still needs to raise its benchmark interest rate to bring down inflation, which she considers too high despite the economy remaining strong. In a speech before the Money Marketeers of New York University on Thursday (19/11), Paulson said controlling inflation must be the Federal Reserve's (Fed) top monetary policy priority. “I see economic growth strengthening and the labour market at full employment. So it is clear that inflation needs to be the monetary policy priority right now,” Paulson said, as quoted by Reuters . She stressed that bringing inflation down requires higher interest rates. In her view, the Fed still has room to continue tightening monetary policy. “The way we bring inflation down is by raising interest rates,” she said, adding that further tightening was still needed. Nevertheless, Paulson believes gradual and consistent interest rate increases are preferable to drastic moves. This approach, she said, would give the economy time to adjust to higher short-term borrowing costs. Paulson, who has voting rights on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) this year, also highlighted the importance of central bank communication in determining the direction of monetary policy. In her view, a shared understanding between the Fed and market participants is more important than providing explicit guidance on the interest rate outlook. “Communication works best when it builds a shared understanding of the policy reaction function. Credibility is very important because people act on messages they believe,” she said. She added that understanding how the Fed responds to the latest economic data could help market participants anticipate the direction of monetary policy without having to rely on detailed guidance from the central bank at all times. Her remarks come as the Fed is changing its approach to communicating with the public. Under Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, the central bank has shortened its FOMC policy statements and established a task force to review how it communicates policy decisions and its economic outlook. Unlike several previous Fed chairs, Warsh has also almost entirely stopped providing guidance on the interest rate outlook. However, several other central bank officials continue to regularly share their views on the direction of monetary policy and economic conditions. Paulson cited the Fed's decision to hold interest rates steady in late October after raising them in September. In her view, markets had anticipated further tightening, so the decision to keep rates unchanged did not leave monetary policy out of step with the needs of the economy. The FOMC is scheduled to hold its next meeting on 8–9 December. Markets broadly expect the Fed to raise interest rates again from their current range of 3.75%–4%. (DK/ZH)

body: The Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4% in October, but its September projections pointed to a hike. Here is what each document says and how it reaches corporate funding costs. The Federal Open Market Committee held the federal funds target range at 3.75% to 4% at its most recent meeting, on October 27 and 28, 2026, by a 10-2 vote. Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. The next decision, with new projections, comes on December 9. Each decision arrives as a package: a policy statement with the vote, an implementation note setting the rates the Fed administers, a press conference by the chair, minutes three weeks later and, at four meetings a year, a Summary of Economic Projections that includes the dot plot. Start with the statement. Its opening paragraphs describe the economy and are revised word by word from meeting to meeting, so the changes count for more than the text itself. In October the committee said economic activity was expanding at a strong pace, productivity growth was strong, capital investment was robust and inflation remained elevated. It said more information would help it set a policy stance to ensure "a timely return of inflation to its 2 percent goal," and added: "The Committee will deliver price stability." Next comes the vote. Dissents show which way the debate is leaning, and both of October's favored tighter policy. Chair Kevin Warsh then took questions. The press conference is where the chair explains how the committee weighs incoming data. The implementation note is the plumbing. Effective October 29, it set the interest rate on reserve balances at 3.90%, the overnight reverse repurchase rate at 3.75%, and the primary credit rate at the discount window and the standing repo rate at 4.0% each. Those administered rates keep the market federal funds rate inside the target range. The dot plot comes with the Summary of Economic Projections in March, June, September and December. Each dot is one participant's view of the midpoint of the appropriate target range at the end of a given year, under what that participant considers appropriate policy. Voters are only part of the group: 12 members voted in October, while 18 participants submitted projections in September 2026. September's dots were hawkish. The median for the end of 2026 was 4.1%, above the current midpoint of 3.875%, implying one more quarter-point increase this year. Two participants placed their 2026 dot at 3.875%, twelve at 4.125% and four at 4.375%. The median was also 4.1% for 2027, then 3.9% for 2028, 3.6% for 2029 and 3.2% in the longer run. The same release shows why. The median projection for inflation measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index was 3.7% for 2026 and 2.3% for 2027, with core inflation at 3.4% this year. Unemployment was projected at 4.1% and growth at 2.3%. The central tendency excludes the three highest and three lowest projections; the range includes all of them. Dots are forecasts, not commitments. They rest on each participant's own assumptions and the information available at the meeting, and they can move by the next release. The minutes, published about three weeks after each meeting, show how widely a view was held. The October minutes came out on November 18. title: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than expected, complicating Fed's inflation fight
summary: The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next move regarding interest rates.
body: Costs for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation. The consumer price index , a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase. Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain. The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%. The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was "around 0.3." Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped. "This was the report the market could least afford to see," said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. "A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer." The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data. Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%. Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%. Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%. At the Fed's October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data. Markets already had been expecting the Fed to hike its benchmark borrowing rate next month, but the inflation data may have sealed the deal. Despite the moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for some 5½ years. "We've been moving up to what historically we'd consider full employment, and the big problem has all been on the inflation side. We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday during an event in his home district. body: Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) shares saw their worst single-day fall in about 22 months amid concerns of the AI boom running out of steam, with slowing growth expectations, margin pressure and questions over hyperscaler spending weighing on investor sentiment. IO Fund’s Beth Kindig argued that investors may be mistaking a temporary pause for a fundamental slowdown, pointing to Nvidia's latest results, expanding AI demand and a valuation that has fallen sharply even as growth expectations remain elevated. Nvidia shares fell more than 14% in Friday’s regular trading, but gained nearly 4% during the afterhours session. Kindig Says Nvidia's Next-Generation AI Chips Are Already Flexing Muscle Nvidia's transition to its Vera Rubin platform appears to be progressing faster than its previous Blackwell ramp, according to Kindig. Rubin generated approximately $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, nearly double Blackwell's $11 billion in its initial quarter. Kindig argued that investors may be overlooking how product transitions have historically affected Nvidia's growth trajectory. During the Blackwell ramp, sequential revenue growth slowed before accelerating again as demand picked up. She suggested that the current transition could follow a similar pattern, with temporary growth moderation being mistaken for a longer-term deterioration in demand. Kindig also points to Nvidia's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook, which implies growth of approximately 75%, up from 70% projected for fiscal 2027 despite a larger revenue base. Kindig noted that the defining characteristic of the AI infrastructure boom remains a supply-constrained market in which demand continues to exceed available capacity. She highlighted that Nvidia's supply-related commitments surged to $390 billion in the third quarter (Q3) of fiscal 2027, up from $119 billion just two quarters earlier. Meanwhile, cloud industry backlog climbed to $2.5 trillion from $2 trillion in just three months. “Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, underscoring the significant multi-year opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia,” said Nvidia’s CFO and interim CEO, Collette Kress. Kindig also pointed to supply constraints elsewhere in the AI ecosystem, including SK Hynix's comments about being effectively sold out through 2029. For her, these figures suggest that the AI infrastructure buildout is far from running out of demand. The decline in AI token prices may be creating a counterintuitive effect, wherein cheaper AI services could drive greater usage, ultimately increasing demand for computing infrastructure. Nvidia reported that token prices have fallen nearly 60% since May, while token consumption has accelerated. Kindig sees this dynamic as an example of “Jevons Paradox,” where improvements in efficiency and lower costs can ultimately lead to greater consumption. She also highlighted the surprising strength of older GPU generations. Hopper GPUs are reportedly being recontracted at up to twice their original prices under multiyear agreements, while B300 rental rates have risen more than 60% since introduction. Kindig argues that AI workloads are increasingly spreading across different GPU generations rather than being concentrated exclusively on the newest hardware, extending the useful economic life of older systems. She believes that is another sign that AI demand remains robust rather than showing signs of saturation.
